<!-- generated from maestro item 906 — do not edit; the board item is the source of truth -->
# jobs.publish silently reroutes an unconfigured channel to "default" — cross-box channel routing is impossible

## Symptom

A multi-box deployment cannot dedicate a jobman channel to one box when the
*publishing* box also runs an engine. `JOBS_CHANNELS` is one setting carrying
two unrelated meanings, and the combination forecloses the obvious topology.

Verified against django-mojo **1.2.61** (what maestro prod runs today).

## The two meanings

1. **What this box's engine consumes.** `job_engine.py:79` —
   `self.channels = channels or JOBS_CHANNELS` — and the engine registers as a
   competing consumer on every channel in that list (`for channel in
   self.channels`, consumer-group registration per channel).
2. **What this box may publish to.** `mojo/apps/jobs/__init__.py:103-106` —
   `publish()` validates the requested channel against the **publisher's own**
   `JOBS_CHANNELS`:

   ```python
   configured_channels = JOB_CHANNELS if isinstance(JOB_CHANNELS, list) else [JOB_CHANNELS]
   if channel not in configured_channels:
       logit.warning("jobs.publish: channel '%s' not in JOBS_CHANNELS, falling back to 'default'", channel)
       channel = "default"
   ```

   The publish **succeeds** on the wrong channel. The caller cannot tell.

## Why that combination is a bug, concretely

Topology: an API box (runs an engine for its own work) wants to publish
box-specific jobs to a worker box's dedicated channel — e.g. maestro's API box
publishing site deploys to a `sites` channel consumed only by the sites box,
whose jobs MUST NOT run anywhere else (they write tenant content to that box's
disk).

- **API box `JOBS_CHANNELS = ["default"]`** → `publish("sites", …)` is silently
  rerouted to `default` → the API box's **own engine** claims the job → it
  fails the box-role guard → the worker box never sees it. The deploy is lost,
  and the publish call reported success.
- **API box `JOBS_CHANNELS = ["default", "sites"]`** → publish routes
  correctly, but the same list drives consumption, so the API box's engine now
  **also subscribes to `sites`** and races the worker box as a competing
  consumer. A random subset of deploys is claimed by the wrong box and fails.

There is no third configuration: the jobs CLI (`cli.py:145,196,240`) reads
`settings.get("JOBS_CHANNELS")` at every engine start and exposes **no
`--channel` override**, so a box cannot consume a narrower set than it
publishes to.

## Consequence

This is why maestro item 393 could not use jobman for site deploys and built a
parallel transport instead (DB queue + Redis nudge + a dedicated worker daemon
— `SiteRevision.status` as source of truth, `aws/sites/worker.py`). The
workaround is fine, but every future box-specific job hits the same wall, and
the silent fallback means a misconfigured channel produces lost/misrouted work
with a success return — only a warning in the publisher's log.

## Fix (either of two shapes; the first is one flag)

1. **Expose the existing per-instance override in the CLI.** `JobEngine`
   already accepts `channels` (`job_engine.py:79`); the CLI never passes it.
   Add `--channels a,b` to the engine-start paths so a box can publish to
   channels it does not consume. Publish-validation then needs its own list —
   see 2 — or simply stops validating.
2. **Split the setting.** e.g. `JOBS_CHANNELS` (consume) +
   `JOBS_PUBLISH_CHANNELS` (allowed publish targets, defaulting to
   "anything"). A channel does not need publisher-side declaration at all:
   Redis streams create on first XADD, and a typo'd channel is better surfaced
   by monitoring an unconsumed stream than by silently running the job on the
   wrong box.
3. **In all cases: stop the silent fallback.** Publishing to an unconfigured
   channel should raise (or at minimum be opt-in-fallback). Rerouting a job to
   a different queue than the caller named — while returning success — turns a
   config typo into misrouted execution instead of an error.

## Acceptance

- A publisher box can `jobs.publish("sites", …)` without its own engine ever
  consuming `sites`.
- An engine can be started on an explicit channel list narrower than (or
  disjoint from) the settings default.
- Publishing to a channel the box may not target is a loud error, not a
  rerouted success.
- Regression test: two engines with disjoint channel lists against one Redis —
  each claims only its own channels' jobs.

## Provenance

Found while investigating maestro's sites deploy architecture (why item 393
bypassed jobman). The original constraint was recorded in maestro's
`planning/built/393.md` Investigation (2026-07-25) and re-verified line-by-line
against 1.2.61 on 2026-07-30. The referenced maestro-side workaround lives in
`apps/mojo/sites/services/hosting.py` + `aws/sites/worker.py`; migrating it
back to jobman was deliberately kept cheap (`enqueue_deploy()` + the daemon
entrypoint) pending this fix.

## Plan

### Objective

`jobs.publish(channel=X)` puts the job on channel X. Always. No validation, no
rerouting. The consume side stays explicit (`JOBS_CHANNELS`, plus a new CLI
override), the cluster-singleton scheduler promotes delayed/retry jobs for
**every** channel in the cluster (not just the lock-winning box's list), and a
queue that holds jobs nobody is consuming raises an incident so operators find
out fast. Each engine also consumes a channel named after its own host, so any
box can be targeted directly with zero configuration.

**Design pivot (owner decision, 2026-07-30):** the first draft of this plan
kept the reroute-to-default as the compat default and added opt-in strict
validation (`JOBS_PUBLISH_CHANNELS` / `JOBS_PUBLISH_STRICT` /
`strict_channel`). The owner overruled it in review: publish-as-named
unconditionally; an unconsumed queue is surfaced by monitoring (the workspec's
own shape-2 argument). All the publish-side validation machinery is dropped;
compatibility is handled on the consume side + docs + a new alert instead
(below).

### Scoping findings that shape the fix

1. **The old fallback was load-bearing.** The framework itself publishes to
   seven named channels most deployments never configure — `cleanup`
   (account/assistant/incident/jobs/logit/shortlink cronjobs),
   `incident_handlers` (incident), `renditions`
   (fileman/models/file.py:652,707), the cert-sync channel (a setting:
   `DNSMAN_CERT_SYNC_CHANNEL`, default `"certs"` —
   dnsman/services/certs.py:48,77), `webhooks` + `webhook_fanout`
   (publish_webhook / account fan-out), `priority` (jobs/rest/jobs.py:395) —
   and three doc pages document the reroute as intended graceful degradation
   (`docs/django_developer/fileman/renditions.md:39`, `dnsman/README.md:202`,
   `dnsman/Certificates.md:131`). Removing the reroute therefore requires:
   (a) the **default** consume list to grow to cover the framework channels
   so unconfigured deployments keep working, (b) an explicit
   breaking-change/upgrade note for deployments that set a narrow
   `JOBS_CHANNELS` by hand, and (c) those three doc pages rewritten (their
   statements become false).
2. **Second latent bug, same root cause: the scheduler.** The Scheduler is a
   cluster singleton (leadership lock, `scheduler.py:157-191`, lock key is
   global not per-channel) but promotes only **its own** `JOBS_CHANNELS`
   (`scheduler.py:29,55,280`). In the target topology (API box `["default"]`,
   sites box `["sites"]`), whichever box wins the lock stalls the other box's
   delayed jobs — and **engine retries**, which also route through the sched
   ZSET (`job_engine.py:718-721`). Fixing publish+engine without the
   scheduler leaves acceptance criterion 1 broken for any delayed or retried
   job. In scope.
3. **Unconsumed jobs eventually expire.** Jobs default to
   `JOBS_DEFAULT_EXPIRES_SEC` (900s in code); a job that sits on an
   unconsumed queue past its expiry is marked `expired` when finally
   consumed. So the cost of a typo'd/unregistered channel is bounded by how
   fast the operator reacts — which is why the unconsumed-queue incident
   alert ships in the same change, not later.
4. **The docs' engine-start command does not exist.**
   `docs/django_developer/jobs/publishing.md` (Channels section) and the
   `mojo/apps/jobs/settings.py` docstring show
   `python manage.py jobs_engine --channels ...` — there is no such
   management command (`mojo/apps/jobs/management/commands/` is empty). The
   real entry points are `python -m mojo.apps.jobs.cli` (no channel arg
   today) and `python -m mojo.apps.jobs.scheduler` (which already has
   `--channels`, `scheduler.py:492` — the CLI wrapper just never passes one).
5. **`jobs.JOB_CHANNELS` is imported by
   `mojo/apps/incident/models/rule.py:183`** (a caller-side copy of the old
   fallback: pre-routes `incident_handlers` → `default` when unconfigured).
   The constant must survive for import compatibility; the pre-check itself
   is deleted (publish-as-named makes it wrong, and the expanded default
   consume list makes it unnecessary).
6. **Hostname is not a channel today.** The engine uses the cleaned hostname
   only for its runner id (`{host}-engine`, `job_engine.py:120-129`),
   heartbeat payload, and per-runner control pub/sub key — nothing consumes a
   host-named queue. Owner asked for it; added as a feature (below).

### Design

**publish() — remove the gate entirely.** Delete the validate/fallback block
(`jobs/__init__.py:100-106`). The named channel is used verbatim for the Job
row, the Redis queue/ZSET, events, and metrics. A falsy channel (`None`/`""`)
raises `ValueError` (it would mint a `...queue:None` key — caller bug, loud).
The `JOB_CHANNELS` module constant stays for import compatibility but publish
no longer reads it. No new settings, no strict flags, no per-call knobs.

**Default consume list grows.** New module constant in
`mojo/apps/jobs/__init__.py`:
`DEFAULT_CHANNELS = ["default", "priority", "cleanup", "incident_handlers",
"renditions", "certs", "webhooks", "webhook_fanout"]` — used as the
`JOBS_CHANNELS` fallback default by the engine, scheduler, CLI, and testit
helpers (replacing the scattered `['default']` literals). Out-of-the-box
deployments therefore consume every channel the framework publishes to —
same effective behavior as today's reroute (one box runs everything), but
jobs ride their named queues. Deployments that set `JOBS_CHANNELS` explicitly
take full control and get the upgrade note. (`certs` covers the *default* of
`DNSMAN_CERT_SYNC_CHANNEL`; overriding that setting means adding your custom
channel to a consumer's list — documented.)

**Hostname channel (new, owner-requested).** Each engine appends its cleaned
hostname (same normalization as the runner id, minus the `-engine` suffix) to
its consume list unless `JOBS_HOSTNAME_CHANNEL = False` (default `True`).
This gives box-targeted publishing with zero configuration:
`jobs.publish(..., channel="sites-box-1")` runs on that box only. Competing
engines on the same host share the host channel (fine — same box). The
scheduler needs no special handling: a delayed host-targeted job reaches the
sched ZSET and the registry like any other channel.

**Unconsumed-queue incident alert (new).** A jobs cron (registered in
`mojo/apps/jobs/cronjobs.py`, every ~5 min) walks the queue keys
(`scan_iter` on `{prefix}:{jobs}:queue:*` — on-demand, manager-style, not in
a hot loop): for each queue with depth > 0 where **no live runner heartbeat**
(`runner:*:hb`, TTL'd JSON whose payload already carries `channels`) lists
that channel, fire `incident.report_event` (category
`jobs:unconsumed_channel`, details: channel, depth, oldest job id). This is
what turns "our incident engine will alert us quickly" from a bespoke ops
setup into a framework guarantee, and it is the safety net that replaces the
old reroute. A consumed-but-busy queue (heartbeat present) never alerts —
that's capacity, a different concern. A box that is down with jobs queued for
it **does** alert — desired.

**Engine CLI**: `cli.py` gains `--channels a,b` and `--runner-id` on
`engine start` / `engine foreground` (threaded into `JobEngine(channels=...,
runner_id=...)` — the constructor already accepts both, `job_engine.py:68-79`);
`--channels` likewise on `scheduler start` / `scheduler foreground` →
`Scheduler(channels=...)`. A small pure helper (`parse_channels_arg`) does
comma-split/strip ONLY and returns `None` when the flag is absent — **no
settings fallback in the CLI**. The CLI start paths stop reading
`JOBS_CHANNELS` themselves (today's `cli.py:145,196,240,282`) and pass the
parsed value (or `None`) straight through; each constructor owns its default
(`JobEngine`: settings list; `Scheduler`: auto mode, below). This wiring is
load-bearing: if the CLI kept passing the settings list, the scheduler would
always look "explicitly pinned" and auto mode would be dead code on the only
production start path (challenge finding). A wiring test asserts both
scheduler start paths construct `Scheduler(channels=None)` when no flag is
given. When `--runner-id` is given, `start_engine_daemon` checks *that
runner's* pidfile instead of the "any engine running → skip" glob
(`is_engine_running`), so a second engine with a distinct runner id and
channel set can coexist on a box.

**Scheduler channel registry (auto mode)**: when constructed with
`channels=None`, the scheduler serves `union(settings JOBS_CHANNELS,
registry)` where the registry is a Redis SET (`{prefix}:sched_registry`, new
`JobKeys.sched_registry()`), refreshed via `SMEMBERS` in the main loop at
most every 5s (time-based guard), wrapped in try/except keeping the last
known list (never crash the loop). The registry is written with one O(1)
`SADD` at the two places that put work into sched ZSETs: `publish()`'s
delayed path and `job_engine._handle_job_failure()`'s retry path. On startup
(auto mode only) the scheduler seeds the registry once by scanning existing
`sched:*` / `sched_broadcast:*` keys (`scan_iter`, the
`manager.get_registered_channels()` pattern, `manager.py:1073-1098`) so
pre-upgrade delayed jobs are covered. A registry SET instead of periodic
scanning because the challenge pass flagged the cost profile: a 5s
`scan_iter` walks the ENTIRE shared Redis keyspace (metrics + settings cache
live there too) inside the leadership-lock holder's loop — on a large
keyspace one refresh could exceed the 2.5s renew interval / 5s lock TTL.
`SMEMBERS` on a handful of channel names is trivial; stale members cost one
empty `zpopmin` pair per cycle. An explicit `channels=[...]` (CLI flag or
constructor) pins the list — no registry; existing tests that construct
`Scheduler(channels=[...])` are unaffected. This makes the lock-winning
scheduler serve the whole cluster's delayed/retry jobs regardless of which
box it runs on. Worst-case promotion delay for a brand-new channel is ~5s +
the existing 250-500ms cycle.

**Test infrastructure**: `testit/helpers.py:_job_channels` and the generated
testproject's `JOBS_CHANNELS` literal (`bin/create_testproject:206`) move to
the expanded default (plus the testproject's `email` test channel) so
`th.run_jobs()` keeps draining framework-channel jobs that previously rode
the reroute onto `default`.

**Unchanged**: engine claim loop (BRPOP over `self.channels` only — already
correct per box), reaper (per-channel on the consuming engine),
`publish_local`, Job/JobEvent models (no schema change → no
`bin/create_testproject` for migrations; it IS re-run for the settings
literal), REST surface and permissions.

### Edge cases

- Falsy channel (`None`/`""`) → `ValueError` before any DB write (loud,
  caller bug — the one publish-time error that remains).
- `JOBS_CHANNELS` given as a bare string → normalized to one-element list
  (existing behavior, kept).
- Colon-bearing or unbounded dynamic channel names: forbidden by docs (the
  engine's channel derivation splits the queue key on `:`; per-channel
  metric slugs are unbounded-cardinality otherwise). The registry SET has no
  key parsing to break.
- Registry Redis errors on refresh → keep the last known list (loop
  survives); seed-scan errors → proceed with settings list.
- Delayed job on a brand-new channel: registered at publish time, picked up
  on the next ≤5s refresh — promotion delay bounded by refresh interval +
  cycle time.
- Stale registry members (a channel no longer used) cost one empty `zpopmin`
  pair per cycle — harmless; the SET stays tiny by construction.
- Two engines, one host: distinct `--runner-id` gives distinct pidfile +
  heartbeat key; both consume the host channel (same box — fine); without
  `--runner-id` the second start is refused exactly as today.
- Worker box down with jobs on its queues (host channel or dedicated) → the
  unconsumed-channel incident fires — desired (that queue has no live
  consumer).
- `ScheduledTask.channel` rows (`jobs/cronjobs.py:77`) with a typo'd channel
  → jobs land on the typo'd queue → alert names it; previously they silently
  ran on `default`.
- Upgrade window: a narrowed deployment that misses the CHANGELOG note finds
  out via the incident within ~5 minutes of the first affected publish, not
  via silently missing work.

- `bin/run_tests --agent` (baseline, step 1; again at step 13)
- `bin/run_tests --agent -t test_jobs.test_channel_routing` during development
- Diagnostics from `var/test_failures.json`, server logs in `testproject/var/`

Covered in step 12; both doc tracks checked, CHANGELOG updated, indexes

### Challenge

An independent fresh-context agent red-teamed the **first draft** (workspec +
plan + challenge ground rules: name untested assumptions, argue the strongest
opposing case, never invent flaws). Eight objections; each verified against
the code before disposition. The design then pivoted on owner review (see
Objective) — dispositions below note what survived the pivot.

1. **Scheduler discovery would be dead code on the CLI start paths**
   (blocks-build) — the draft had the CLI fall back to the settings list, so
   `Scheduler(channels=<list>)` always looked explicitly pinned and auto mode
   never engaged on the production start path (`cli.py:196-203,282-289`),
   while the planned test constructed `Scheduler()` directly and stayed
   green. **Disposition: amended, survives pivot** — CLI passes `None` when
   the flag is absent; wiring test added.
2. **Periodic full-keyspace `scan_iter` inside the lock-holder's loop can
   starve the 5s leadership lock** (weakens-design) — the jobs adapter is the
   framework-wide Redis (metrics + settings cache share it); `SCAN MATCH`
   filters replies, not the walk. Verified against
   `scheduler.py:30,62-63,253-262`. **Disposition: amended, survives pivot**
   — registry SET + one-time seed scan replaces periodic scanning.
3. **The settings API for the new publish-side reads was unpinned**
   (weakens-design) — `settings.get` would hit DB-backed `account.Setting`
   with no negative caching per publish. **Disposition: mooted by pivot** —
   publish no longer reads any routing settings. (The finding stands as
   recorded knowledge: `setting.py:265-280` global-scope misses don't
   backfill.)
4. **The seam-mock left the real settings-read path untested** —
   **mooted by pivot**: there is no publish-side settings read left to test;
   the regression test now exercises the real publish path with no patching
   at all.
5. **rule.py's preserved pre-check contradicts the new setting** — verified
   (`rule.py:183`). **Disposition: superseded by pivot** — the pre-check is
   deleted outright; `incident_handlers` is published unconditionally and
   consumed by the expanded default list.
6. **Acceptance criterion 3 renegotiated + box-wide strict needs framework
   channels enumerated** — the draft delivered "loud error" only opt-in.
   **Disposition: superseded by pivot** — there is no publish-time error at
